newsitem.title: USA: IMF finance ministers set to launch debt plan.
newsitem.headline: IMF finance ministers set to launch debt plan.

text.p: International finance ministers planned to launch a debt relief initiative on Monday that is meant to bring economic growth to the world's poorest countries, mainly in Africa.

The initiative, expected to be endorsed later on Monday by the International Monetary Fund's Development Committee, aims to lift the burden for countries that must spend all the benefits of economic growth on debt service charges.

"We now have the comprehensive framework required to address the debt problems of these countries by reducing on a case-by-case basis debt burdens to manageable levels," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said.

"The...initiave, combined with strong policy reforms, will help put some fo the world's poorest countries on a sound footing for future development and growth," he told ministers during the annual meeting here of the IMF and World Bank.

Ministers have yet to say which countries are likely to benefit first from the initiative, which is being launched jointly by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and Paris Club of creditor nations.

On Saturday, the Paris Club said it was willing to write-off debt of up to 80 percent for low-income countries on a case-by-case basis compared to 67 percent currently available under so-called Naples terms.

It will provide the improved debt relief in conjuction with the IMF and World Bank, whose lending to the Third World has in itself become part of the problem for countries that the multilateral institutions originally set out to help.

Among those likely to be first in line, according to British officials, are Uganda, the Ivory Coast, Ethiopia and Guyana. Other possible beneficiaries include Bolivia, Mali and Burkina Faso, they said.
Other countries cited by some as facing unsustainable levels of debt include Guinea Bissau, Mozambique, Sao Tome, Sudan, Zaire and Zambia.
Creditor sources said however that no decision had been made on which countries would benefit first, though Ethiopia is expected to hold debt talks with the Paris Club shortly.
"People can say who they would prefer to benefit first. But no decision has been taken to date on a list of countries," one creditor source said.
Formal launching of the initiative on Monday was expected however to pave the way for detailed work by the IMF and World Bank on the plan.
Rubin said on Sunday he expected the new debt relief initiative to prove as important for poor countries as the 1989 Brady plan was for middle-income developing nations.
That debt-reduction plan, named after former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, helped restore the economies of many Latin American countries to good health.
